blocks.text: Honey is commended above all for the sweetness of its taste. Hence the Son of Sirach, above, on the bee: Ἀρχὴ γλυκασμάτων ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῆς [Archē glykasmatōn ho karpos autēs], The beginning of sweet things (or, is supremely sweet) is its fruit. And Samson, in the riddle he put to the Philistines at the wedding feast, Iud. XIV, 14. Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness: that is, honey out of the lion. For we have already learned that honey was found in the body of the lion. The Hebrew has בגוית האריה, the Greek Ἐν ςόματι τοῦ λέοντος [En stomati tou leontos]; but this should be corrected to ἐν σώματι [en sōmati]. Likewise in verse 9, where the Complutensian edition and the recent Paris edition read Ἐκ τῆς ἕξεως τοῦ λέοντος ἐξεῖλεν τὸ μέλι [Ek tēs hexeōs tou leontos exeilen to meli], I would restore ἐκ τῆς ἰξύος [ek tēs ixyos], from the loin, as the rendering of גויה, since גו is commonly taken for the back or rear, where the loins are. But the less frequent word ἰξύος [ixyos] was changed into ἕξεως [hexeōs] through the ignorance of scribes, whose habit it is to corrupt whatever they do not understand. However that may be, since Samson had taken honey out of a lion's body, a thing otherwise without precedent, he drew from it the subject of a griphus or riddle. For it was the custom among the ancients to propose questions at banquets, in the solving of which their wits were exercised. [III, 384] Clearchus calls such a question a griphus, and in Athenaeus defines it thus: Γρίφος πρόβλημά ἐστι παιστικὸν, προστακτικὸν τοῦ διὰ ζητήσεως εὑρεῖν τῇ διανοίᾳ τὸ προβληθὲν, τιμῆς ἢ ἐπιζημίου χάριν εἰρημένον [Griphos problēma esti paistikon, prostaktikon tou dia zētēseōs heurein tē dianoia to problēthen, timēs ē epizēmiou charin eirēmenon]. A griphus is a playful problem, by which one is bidden to find out by searching of the mind what has been proposed, put forward for the sake of a reward or a penalty. And that such were customarily proposed to guests at table, Athenaeus shows at length in book 10. Julius [col. 523] Pollux also mentions them in book 6, chapter 19, where he distinguishes the riddles and griphi of drinking companions, holding that the former were always jocular, the latter sometimes serious. His words are: Τῶν μὲν συμποτικῶν αἴνιγμα καὶ γρῖφος· τὸ μὲν παιδιὰν εἶχεν, ὁ δὲ γρῖφος καὶ σπουδήν [Tōn men sympotikōn ainigma kai griphos; to men paidian eichen, ho de griphos kai spoudēn]. He goes on to say that the one who solved it was given a dish of meat, κρεῶν τινα περιφορὰν [kreōn tina periphoran], just as ἅλμης ποτήριον [halmēs potērion], a cup of brine, was given to be drunk by the one who could not solve it. Other rewards too, and likewise other penalties, customary among the Greeks, may be read in Athenaeus in the place cited. Gellius, book 18, ch. 2, reports that something of the sort was practised by Romans at Athens during the Saturnalia: Several of us Romans who had come to Greece and attended the same lectures and the same teachers used to meet at the same dinner. Then the one whose turn it was to provide the little dinner would set as the prize for solving a question a book by an old writer, either Greek or Latin, and a crown woven of laurel; and he would ask as many questions as there were men present. When he had set them all out, the lot assigned the question and the order of speaking. If the question was solved, the man was presented with the crown and the prize; if it was not solved, it passed to the one who came next by lot. And this was kept up in turn around the circle. If no one untied the knot of the question, the prize itself and the crown were dedicated to the god whose festival it was. But nothing establishes the antiquity of the custom so much as what we read of Samson: that he proposed to his thirty guests a riddle to be solved within the seven days of the feast, on the condition that, if they solved it, they would receive as a prize thirty linen garments and as many changes of clothing; if not, they themselves would give them. The riddle was this: Out of the eater came forth food, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. In these words, as food is set against the eater, so sweetness is set against the strong. Yet these do not seem to be opposites. For the opposite of strong is unwarlike or weak; the opposite of sweet is sharp or bitter. But sometimes these are confused, and bitter is taken for strong, and sharp for both. Thus in Arabic مرة [mirra] mirra, that is, strength, and مرير [marīr] merir, that is, robust, vigorous, come from the verb مر [marra] marra, which means to be bitter. And in Latin a man who is strong is called acer [sharp], as in Aeneid book 8:
Or would you hesitate to call bold Turnus to battle?

On which passage Servius says: ACREM TURNUM) strong. And properly with us acer is what δεινὸς [deinos] is among the Greeks. For it can mean strong, and vehement, and harsh, and bitter. Nonius likewise: Acrem, strong, Aen. book 7 (read book 8). Rightly therefore Junius at Iudic. XIV, 14: From the sharp came forth sweetness.
